name: Software Architecture with C++ 2E: binary search (std::ranges::lower_bound) versus linear scan (std::ranges::find) in a sorted vector
baseline: std::ranges::find (linear scan) on a sorted std::vector<int>
workload: Google Benchmark of std::ranges::lower_bound against std::ranges::find on a sorted std::vector<int> of 1000 to 10,000,000 elements; variant main_1 looks up the value 2137 in 10M elements, variant main_4 looks up needles at 1/8, 1/2, last and one-past-last positions of 1e3, 1e5 and 1e7 element vectors.
claimed_speedup: Book sample run (relayed via seed lead, not on a repo page): binary search 24.2 ns versus linear search 471 ns for the 2137 needle in 10M elements; with the needle at the end of 10M elements about 24 ns versus 2.8 ms. Ratios (derived from the relayed numbers): about 19x and about 117,000x.
compiler_and_flags: Repo README for Chapter13 requires a Conan profile of GCC 15, gnu20, libstdc++11 and a CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so CMake's default GCC Release flags, normally -O3 -DNDEBUG, which the repo does not spell out); targets set cxx_std_20 (Google Benchmark 1.9.4 via Conan, benchmark_1..4) or cxx_std_23 (Catch2 3.12.0 and nanobench 4.3.11 variants). The compiler and flags of the book's actual run are not stated.
hardware: Book run reported only as a 20-thread 2022 MHz CPU with 48 KiB L1d and 24 MiB L3 (Google Benchmark context block, relayed via lead); no CPU model.
stars_or_usage: 74 stars, 22 forks; Packt companion repository of the book Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed.
tradeoffs: Binary search needs sorted input and random access (O(log n) versus O(n)); for tiny vectors a linear scan can win because of branch prediction and cache locality, which the 1000-element points in benchmark_3 and benchmark_4 are meant to show. Not a library: a std algorithm choice.
caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page I opened (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. The comparison is an algorithmic-complexity truism (logarithmic versus linear on sorted data), not a faster implementation of the same algorithm; the speedup grows with n by construction. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU model are unstated and the repo holds code only. In the Google Benchmark and Catch2 variants the vector is built outside the timed region; the nanobench_doctest variant builds the vector inside the timed lambda (main_4), so it times construction as well as the search. The same benchmark is written three times (Google Benchmark, Catch2, nanobench with doctest) and only the Google Benchmark numbers are given in the book. Repo files opened: Chapter13/microbenchmarking/benchmark/main_1..4.cpp and CMakeLists.txt, catch2/main_1.cpp and main_4.cpp, nanobench_doctest/main_4.cpp and CMakeLists.txt, Chapter13/conanfile.py and README.md.

name: Software Architecture with C++ 2E: computed-goto bytecode dispatch versus a single switch
baseline: switch-based bytecode interpreter loop (single large switch in a while loop, same repo)
workload: Catch2 BENCHMARK_ADVANCED of two seven-opcode toy stack-less VMs (HALT, INC, DEC, MUL2, DIV2, REM2, NEG on one int64 accumulator), switch_vm::bytecode_interpreter against computed_goto_vm::bytecode_interpreter (GCC labels-as-values), both run on the same randomly generated array of 2^24 opcodes.
claimed_speedup: Book reports the computed-goto VM about 23% faster than the single switch, mean about 1.41 ns versus 1.82 ns (relayed via seed lead, not on a repo page); time ratio 1.82/1.41 = about 1.29x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Repo: optimization_2 target is built only when not MSVC, with cxx_std_23, Catch2 3.12.0, Chapter13 Conan profile GCC 15 gnu20 libstdc++11 and a CMake Release build (CMake default flags, normally -O3 -DNDEBUG on GCC, not spelled out). The compiler and flags of the book's run are not stated.
stars_or_usage: 74 stars, 22 forks; Packt companion repository of the book Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed.
tradeoffs: Computed goto is a GCC/Clang extension (labels as values), not standard C++, and is excluded from the MSVC build; the dispatch table has no opcode bounds check, so an invalid opcode is undefined behaviour while the switch version has a default case. Per-opcode replicated indirect jumps help branch prediction on real programs.
caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page I opened (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. Harness defect visible in the source: opcodes are drawn uniformly from 0 to OP_SENTINEL (6), and OP_HALT is 0, so each of the 2^24 slots is HALT with probability 1/7 and both interpreters return at the first HALT. A timed call therefore runs only a short prefix of the array (expected about 7 opcodes), the same prefix on every iteration, which a branch predictor can learn; it does not exercise a long random dispatch stream as the 2^24 size suggests. The prefix also changes between runs because the generator is seeded from std::random_device. The switch version carries a default-case range check that the computed-goto version lacks, so part of the gap is the missing bounds check. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU unstated. Only one program per VM, no real bytecode workload, no comparison with a real interpreter such as CPython. The book also notes CPython moved from switch to computed goto in 2008 and to a tail-call interpreter in 2025, faster in some scenarios and slower in others (per the lead; not opened). Repo files opened: Chapter13/optimization/main_2.cpp and CMakeLists.txt, Chapter13/conanfile.py and README.md.

name: Software Architecture with C++ 2E: tail-recursive Fibonacci with musttail versus naive recursion
baseline: naive double-recursive Fibonacci (same repo; also iterative Fibonacci as a second reference)
workload: Google Benchmark of iterative, plain-recursive and musttail tail-recursive factorial (n = 32768 and 65536) and Fibonacci (n = 16 to 32, doubling) over uint64_t, with DoNotOptimize on the result.
claimed_speedup: Book reports Fibonacci(32): naive recursion about 2,389,913 ns, tail-recursive about 6.94 ns, iterative about 6.74 ns; factorial 32768 and 65536: all three variants about equal, 20 to 40 microseconds (relayed via seed lead, not on a repo page). Ratio naive/tail-recursive about 344,000x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Repo: optimization_1 target, cxx_std_20, Google Benchmark 1.9.4, Chapter13 Conan profile GCC 15 gnu20 libstdc++11 and a CMake Release build (CMake default flags, normally -O3 -DNDEBUG on GCC, not spelled out). The compiler and flags of the book's run are not stated.
stars_or_usage: 74 stars, 22 forks; Packt companion repository of the book Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed.
tradeoffs: musttail forces a guaranteed tail call (Clang attribute, GCC 15 and later via its own attribute) and fails to compile if the call cannot be a tail call; constant stack use, but the attribute is non-standard and the function signatures must match.
caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page I opened (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. The Fibonacci speedup is not caused by musttail: the baseline is the exponential-time double recursion while the tail-recursive version is a linear accumulator loop, so the 2.39 ms versus 6.94 ns gap is an algorithm change, and the tail-recursive version only matches the iterative one (6.94 versus 6.74 ns). The only same-algorithm comparison, factorial, shows the three variants about equal, i.e. no speedup from musttail. The musttail macro tests only __has_cpp_attribute(clang::musttail) and the unscoped musttail, so on GCC it may expand to nothing and the 'musttail' variant is then ordinary optimizer-dependent tail recursion (not checked against the book's compiler). Overflowing uint64_t factorial results are meaningless but harmless to timing. Category is a best fit only: this is a recursion microbenchmark, not a VM measurement; the technique matters to interpreter design (CPython tail-call interpreter) but nothing here runs a bytecode VM. Keep flagged; a verifier may retier to D. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU unstated. Repo files opened: Chapter13/optimization/main_1.cpp and CMakeLists.txt, Chapter13/conanfile.py and README.md.
